title: Don't let them distract you
hook: let neither wealth nor children distract you from remembering Allah (63:9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nifaq, and your line was not propped up. What did you do where no one could see it? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

A parent stands in prayer. Behind them, a toddler is narrating a cartoon at full volume. The phone on the shelf buzzes: a client, an invoice, the bank. Somewhere in the middle of the second unit, the parent realizes they've been planning dinner. None of these things are bad. The child is loved. The work feeds the child. That's exactly what makes them so good at pulling attention away. Surah Al-Munafiqun, after its warnings, turns to the believers and names those two pulls.

Verse nine. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah." The verb is tulhikum, from the root l-h-w, the same root as lahw, the amusement we met in Surah Al-Hadid two weeks ago. Distraction and amusement are the same family: whatever fills your attention so completely that something more important slips out. And notice what the verse names. Not sins. Wealth and children, two things the Qur'an elsewhere calls the adornment of worldly life. The danger isn't in them. It's in how easily they can take up the whole field of view. Surah At-Takathur says it in one line: the rivalry for more distracts you, until you visit the graves. Same root, same pull. Then verse ten turns urgent. Spend from what God has provided, before death comes to one of you and he says: my Lord, if only you'd give me a little more time, I would give in charity and be among the righteous. Verse eleven answers: God does not delay a soul when its term has come. So the verse doesn't say: have less, love less. It says: remember through it. The parent doesn't stop being a parent in prayer. The worker doesn't stop working. But somewhere in the noise, there is a thread back to God, and the verse asks believers not to let it drop. Those who do, it says, are the losers.
screen: `TULHIKUM: FROM L-H-W.` · `WEALTH AND CHILDREN, NOT SINS.` · `IF ONLY I HAD A LITTLE MORE TIME.` · `REMEMBER THROUGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: a phone-free prayer. Put your phone in another room, or face down and silent, out of reach. If you pray, pray your next prayer this way, and notice what pulls at you. If you don't, sit now, without it, for the length of the bell. Each time your mind runs to the screen, the inbox, the next errand, notice the pull, name it gently, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Takathur: the rivalry for more, named in Surah At-Takathur as the same pull Surah Al-Munafiqun warns wealth and children can become. Today's word.
Your line: remember through it all. Today, in the busiest moment of your day, find one breath to remember, right there in the noise. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to pray with presence of heart, and some silence phones and choose a quiet place; 63:9–11 is recited as a reminder to give in charity before death comes.

original.say: laa TUL-hi-kum am-WAA-lu-kum wa laa aw-LAA-du-kum
original.note: Arabic: let not your wealth nor your children distract you. tulhi is from l-h-w.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning against loving money and family too much.
what it means: a warning about attention: good things can fill the whole view and crowd out remembrance.
what a scholar hears: tulhikum from l-h-w, as in lahw (57:20) and alhakum at-takathur (102:1); 18:46 calls wealth and children the adornment of worldly life; 63:10–11 on the deathbed regret.
